title: Telling, asking, and three levels of politeness
goal: Give commands and requests at Urdu's three levels of politeness, and recognize when each one is used.
bekal: forming commands for تو، تم، and آپ
asking for help without sounding bossy
telling someone not to do something with مت and نہ

dialogs.title: مکالمہ — باورچی خانے میں
dialogs.intro: Hasan's mom is teaching Budi how to make Pakistani tea. The kitchen is busy, and commands are flying.

lines.speaker: امی:
lines.text: بودی بیٹا، ادھر آئیے۔ چائے بنانا سیکھیے!
lines.baca: Būdī beṭā, idhar āiye. chāe banānā sīkhiye!
lines.id: Budi, dear, come here. Learn to make tea!
lines.literal: Budi son, here come-please. tea make learn-please!

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: جی، بالکل۔ مجھے کیا کرنا ہے؟
lines.baca: jī, bilkul. mujhe kyā karnā hai?
lines.id: Yes, of course. What should I do?
lines.literal: yes, exactly. to-me what do is?

lines.speaker: امی:
lines.text: پہلے پانی ابالیے۔ پھر چائے کی پتی ڈالیے۔
lines.baca: pahle pānī ubāliye. phir chāe kī pattī ḍāliye.
lines.id: First boil the water. Then add the tea leaves.
lines.literal: first water boil-please. then tea of(f) leaves put-in-please.

lines.speaker: امی:
lines.text: دو چمچ۔ ہاں، اتنی۔ اب دودھ ڈالیے۔
lines.baca: do chamach. hāñ, itnī. ab dūdh ḍāliye.
lines.id: Two spoonfuls. Yes, that much. Now add the milk.
lines.literal: two spoons. yes, that-much(f). now milk put-in-please.

lines.speaker: امی:
lines.text: تم بیٹھو اور دیکھو۔ ابھی ہاتھ مت لگاؤ۔
lines.baca: tum baiṭho aur dekho. abhī hāth mat lagāo.
lines.id: You sit and watch. Don't touch anything yet.
lines.literal: you sit and watch. now hand don't touch.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.id: When do I add the sugar?

lines.speaker: امی:
lines.text: آخر میں۔ اور آہستہ ہلائیے، جلدی نہ کیجیے۔
lines.baca: āḵir meñ. aur āhista hilāiye, jaldī na kījiye.
lines.id: At the end. And stir slowly, don't rush.
lines.literal: end at. and slowly stir-please, hurry don't do-please.

lines.speaker: امی:
lines.text: واہ! بہت اچھی ہے۔ آپ نے جلدی سیکھ لیا۔
lines.baca: vāh! bahut achchhī hai. āp ne jaldī sīkh liyā.
lines.id: Wow! It's really good. You learn fast.
lines.literal: wow! very good(f) is. you (ne) quickly learned taken.

notes: **Three command forms for three pronouns.** For تو: the bare root — کر، جا، بیٹھ. For تم: root + ـو — کرو، جاؤ، بیٹھو. For آپ: root + ـیے — کیجیے، جائیے، بیٹھیے. The choice follows the rule from unit 1: when in doubt, use the آپ form.

**Hasan's mom uses the آپ form with Budi and the تم form with her own son.** Notice آئیے and ڈالیے for the guest, while بیٹھو and دیکھو are for Hasan. The difference isn't about age but about closeness — and as a guest, you'll almost always be given the آپ form.

**Four irregular آپ commands.** The command of کرنا is کیجیے, not کریے · of لینا it's لیجیے · of دینا it's دیجیے · and of پینا it's پیجیے. The rest are regular: from جانا comes جائیے · from آنا comes آئیے · from بیٹھنا comes بیٹھیے · and from کھانا comes کھائیے.

**Telling someone not to do something uses مت, not نہیں.** مت جاؤ ("don't go"). With the gentler آپ form, use **نہ**: جلدی نہ کیجیے ("don't rush"). Using نہیں in a command is a mistake people hear right away.

**An even politer form: root + ـیے گا.** For example بیٹھیے گا and آئیے گا. It isn't a future command but a very gentle request — used with guests, elders, and bosses. Its companion is برائے مہربانی ("please"), which can be added to any command.

**The terms بیٹا and بیٹی are used far beyond the family.** Older people call any young person بیٹا (male) or بیٹی (female), and it's a sign of affection, not condescension. Being called that by your host is a sign you've been accepted.

grammars.title: Three levels of command
body: The rightmost column is the one you'll use almost all the time. You need to **recognize** the other two so you understand when you're told to do something, even if you don't use them yourself.
after: Telling someone not to: مت + the تم form (مت جاؤ) or نہ + the آپ form (نہ جائیے). For firmer, official prohibitions — on public signs, for example — the dictionary form is used: یہاں سگریٹ نہ پیئیں.

grammars.title: Asking without ordering
body: The آپ command is already polite, but real requests are usually wrapped even more gently. The four ways below go from the most direct to the gentlest.

head: Way
Example
Feel
rows: کیا آپ دروازہ بند کر سکتے ہیں؟
Please have a seat. — very polite

after: Answering a request: جی ضرور ("yes, of course") · ابھی کرتا ہوں ("I'll do it right now") · معاف کیجیے، میں نہیں کر سکتا ("sorry, I can't").

⚠️ The word مہربانی appears in many polite expressions: برائے مہربانی (please), آپ کی مہربانی (that's very kind of you), مہربانی فرمائیے (would you kindly). Its root is the same as مہربان, which you've known since unit 2.

blocks.title: Making چائے, and why it matters
items: Pakistani tea is boiled, not steeped: water and milk are cooked together with the tea leaves, and sugar goes in at the end. The commands are exactly like the ones in the dialog — understand them once, and you can follow any Urdu recipe.

Turning down tea in a Pakistani home is almost impossible, and you'd better not try. The offer will be repeated three times. If you really can't: بہت شکریہ، لیکن ابھی نہیں۔ ("thank you so much, but not right now") — and still take a small cup.
Praising after you drink: چائے بہت اچھی ہے۔ ("the tea is lovely") · آپ کے ہاتھ میں ذائقہ ہے۔ ("there's flavor in your hands") — a classic compliment for a cook, and it's sure to make your host smile.

exercises.prompt: Translate into Urdu. Use the polite form (آپ).
Put the words in the right order.

answers: بیٹھیے۔ — برائے مہربانی دروازہ بند کیجیے۔ — جلدی نہ کیجیے۔ — آہستہ بولیے۔ — چائے لیجیے۔
دروازہ بند کیجیے۔ — ابھی مت جاؤ۔ — جلدی نہ کیجیے۔ — برائے مہربانی آہستہ بولیے۔ — چائے لیجیے۔
wave: Memorize the five آپ commands you'll need most: آئیے، بیٹھیے، سنیے، کیجیے، دیجیے. These five words open almost every polite conversation.
